passage:
I'm Chinmay, Kalyani's big brother. Yesterday I watched her toddle towards the stove while Mummy was cooking.
She reached for the shiny knob. Mummy said, “No, Kalyani. Hot.” Firm, not loud.
Kalyani's hand stopped in the air. She looked at Mummy, then shook her own head. “No-no.”
Later she walked past the stove again, looked at the knob, looked at Mummy, and walked on. I think she remembered.

qa.q: What did Kalyani reach for?
qa.a: She reached for the shiny knob on the stove.

qa.q: What might Kalyani have felt when her hand stopped in the air?
qa.a: She was probably unsure and a little surprised, checking Mummy's face to understand the “no.”

qa.q: How could the family help Kalyani learn this rule?
qa.a: They could keep saying “No, hot” calmly each time and move her away gently if she reaches again.

qa.q: How does Chinmay see his sister's reaction?
qa.a: Chinmay is interested and a little proud, thinking she remembered the rule.

grounding: An older brother sees his toddler sister respond to a prohibition and remember it.

passage:
Monday: Omkar, eighteen months old, grabbed the dog's tail. Bruno yelped. Mehak lifted Omkar away. “No. Gentle hands.” Omkar cried.
Thursday: Omkar crawled to Bruno, reached for the tail, stopped, and looked back at his mother. Mehak shook her head. He pulled his hand back.
Sunday: Omkar sat by Bruno and patted his back softly. “Gen-tle,” he said. Bruno wagged.

qa.q: What did Omkar grab on Monday?
qa.a: He grabbed the dog's tail.

qa.q: How did Omkar feel when he was lifted away on Monday?
qa.a: He felt upset and cried when his mother stopped him.

qa.q: What in Mehak's approach helped Omkar learn?
qa.a: She gave the same short rule every time, “Gentle hands,” and showed him what to do instead.

qa.q: How does Bruno experience the change by Sunday?
qa.a: Bruno is patted softly instead of having his tail pulled, so he wags and feels safe.

grounding: Over a week a toddler learns that pulling the dog's tail is not allowed and pats gently instead.

passage:
On Diwali evening, Afreen lit a row of diyas on the balcony of their Lucknow flat. Two-year-old Kashish toddled over, eyes shining, and reached out.
“No, Kashish. Hot,” said Afreen, holding her hand gently.
Kashish looked at the flames, then at her mother. She pulled her hand back and pointed. “Hot! No!”
“Yes. We look, we don't touch.”
Kashish squatted down and watched the flames dance, hands tucked in her lap.

qa.q: Where did Afreen light the diyas?
qa.a: On the balcony of their Lucknow flat.

qa.q: How did Kashish feel when she saw the diyas?
qa.a: She felt excited and curious, with shining eyes.

qa.q: What did Afreen do that helped Kashish understand the rule?
qa.a: She held her hand gently, used a clear short word, and explained they look but don't touch.

qa.q: What would change if Afreen had shouted instead?
qa.a: Kashish might have been frightened and cried, and learned less about why the flames are not allowed.

grounding: A toddler responds to a prohibition near Diwali lamps and repeats the rule herself.

passage:
Every evening at bath time in their Bengaluru flat, Pradeep sang the same old Kannada rhyme his mother had sung to him.
Two-year-old Eshaan splashed and waited for the part where the elephant falls in the water. Before Pradeep could sing it, Eshaan shouted, “Aane! Dhapp!” and slapped the water.
Pradeep laughed. “You remember!”
Eshaan grinned, then pointed at the towel. “Ajji towel!” It was the one his grandmother had sent.

qa.q: Which part of the rhyme did Eshaan wait for?
qa.a: He waited for the part where the elephant falls in the water.

qa.q: How did Eshaan feel during the rhyme?
qa.a: He was excited and happy, splashing and shouting the words before his father.

qa.q: How can Pradeep keep this language alive for Eshaan?
qa.a: He can keep singing Kannada songs every day and use Kannada words for everyday things like bath and towel.

qa.q: How might Eshaan's grandmother feel hearing about this?
qa.a: She would probably feel touched and proud that the rhyme she sang is being passed on 🤍

grounding: A toddler absorbs his family's mother tongue through a bath-time rhyme.

passage:
“Thomas, what's this?” Ammachi held up a soft appam.
“Appam!”
“And what do we say before we eat?”
Two-year-old Thomas folded his tiny hands. “Ammen!”
Farhan laughed from the stove. “Not Amen yet, monu. First the prayer.”
Ammachi sang the short grace in Malayalam. Thomas swayed and hummed along, then shouted, “Ammen!” at the end, exactly on time.
“Good boy,” said Ammachi. “Now, stew or sugar?”
“Sugar!”

qa.q: What did Ammachi hold up?
qa.a: She held up a soft appam.

qa.q: How did Thomas feel when he shouted “Ammen!” on time?
qa.a: He felt proud and happy to be part of the family prayer.

qa.q: How could the family help Thomas learn more of the grace?
qa.a: They could keep singing it at every meal and let him join in the parts he knows.

qa.q: How does Farhan see Thomas's early “Amen”?
qa.a: Farhan is amused and fond, gently correcting him while laughing.

grounding: A toddler absorbs language, prayer and food rituals at the family breakfast table.

passage:
Daycare note, Baisakhi week. Teacher: Lokesh.
Today we played dhol music for the festival. Baljeet (two) jumped up at once, lifted his shoulders up and down in bhangra style and shouted, “Balle balle!” The other children copied him.
At snack time he showed me his tiffin. “Pinni! Biji made.” He offered me a crumb.
Next step: I'll ask families to send one song from home next week 🎶

qa.q: What did Baljeet shout?
qa.a: He shouted, “Balle balle!”

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel when the dhol music played?
qa.a: He was delighted and full of energy, jumping up to dance.

qa.q: Why is asking families to send songs a good idea?
qa.a: It brings each child's home songs and language into class, strengthening their sense of identity.

qa.q: How might Baljeet's Biji feel hearing he shared her pinni?
qa.a: She would probably feel proud and happy that he loves the food she makes.

grounding: A daycare teacher notes a toddler's festival dance, words and food as signs of absorbed culture.

passage:
At the wedding in their village near Jhansi, the brass band started up, and two-year-old Divyansh clapped his hands over his ears and screamed.
His baby cousin slept straight through it on an aunt's shoulder.
Uma picked Divyansh up and carried him out behind the cowshed, where it was quieter. She hummed softly. He took his hands off his ears and leaned on her.
“You don't like loud things,” she murmured. “That's okay. We'll watch from here.”

qa.q: Where did Uma carry Divyansh?
qa.a: She carried him out behind the cowshed, where it was quieter.

qa.q: How did Divyansh feel when the band started?
qa.a: He was overwhelmed and frightened by the loud noise, covering his ears and screaming.

qa.q: What did Uma do that suited Divyansh's temperament?
qa.a: She took him somewhere quieter and hummed softly instead of forcing him to stay.

qa.q: How might Divyansh's reaction differ from his cousin's, and why?
qa.a: His cousin slept through it because each child has a different sensitivity to noise.

grounding: A mother responds to her toddler's sensitivity to loud noise at a village wedding.

passage:
At the Saturday playgroup in Hanoi, Kwame ran straight to the sandpit, threw sand in the air, and laughed.
Bao, the same age, stood at the edge holding his father's leg. He watched for ten minutes. Then he touched the sand with one finger. Then he sat down, slowly.
“He takes his time,” Bao's father said to Kwame's mother.
“Kwame never does,” she laughed.
By the end, both boys were filling the same bucket.

qa.q: How long did Bao watch before touching the sand?
qa.a: He watched for ten minutes.

qa.q: How was Bao feeling at the edge of the sandpit?
qa.a: He felt cautious and a bit unsure, holding his father's leg while he watched.

qa.q: How can Bao's father support Bao's temperament?
qa.a: He can let Bao warm up at his own pace without pushing, as he did.

qa.q: How do the parents see the difference between their boys?
qa.a: They see it calmly and with humour, accepting that each boy has his own way.

grounding: Two toddlers with different temperaments approach a new sandpit in their own way.

passage:
I'm Sudha, Arnab's mashi. On the first day of Durga Puja, I watched Arnab, two, in his new silk kurta.
He pulled at the collar, scratched his neck, then threw himself on the floor and wailed.
I took the kurta off and put him in his soft cotton vest. He stopped crying almost at once and ran to see the drums.
Maybe the silk scratched. I can't say for sure. But he loves the dhak.

qa.q: What did Sudha put Arnab in instead of the kurta?
qa.a: Sudha put him in his soft cotton vest.

qa.q: How did Arnab feel in his new silk kurta?
qa.a: He seemed uncomfortable and upset, pulling at it and wailing.

qa.q: What can Arnab's family do next Puja?
qa.a: They could choose soft cotton clothes for him so he can enjoy the festival.

qa.q: What would change if Sudha had left the silk kurta on?
qa.a: Arnab might have stayed upset and itchy and missed enjoying the dhak drums.

grounding: An aunt notices a toddler's sensitivity to scratchy clothes during Durga Puja.

passage:
“Ritu won't eat,” said Nitin's wife, holding the spoon. “Give her your phone. The rhyme video works.”
Nitin looked at Ritu, eighteen months old, pushing the bowl away.
“Wait. Let me try.” He sat opposite her. “Machli jal ki rani hai!” He wiggled his hand like a fish.
Ritu stared. Then she wiggled her hand too.
“Jeevan uska paani hai!”
Ritu laughed and opened her mouth for the spoon.

qa.q: What did Nitin wiggle like a fish?
qa.a: He wiggled his hand like a fish.

qa.q: How did Ritu feel when her father sang the rhyme?
qa.a: She was delighted and engaged, laughing and copying his hand.

qa.q: Why was singing live better than handing over the phone?
qa.a: Nitin could watch and respond to Ritu, so she joined in and learned instead of just watching.

qa.q: How might Nitin's wife see the live rhyme?
qa.a: She may be pleasantly surprised that it worked as well as the video.

grounding: A father chooses a live rhyme over a phone video to engage his toddler at mealtime.

passage:
Daycare note, Tuesday. Teacher: Maria.
Kishore's parents asked if cartoons would help his words. Today I read our duck picture book with him on my lap. I pointed and said “duck” and quacked. He watched my mouth, then pointed and said “Duh!” Three times.
After last week's cartoons, no new words.
Next step: I told his parents a short cartoon is fine if they watch with him and talk about it 😊

qa.q: What book did Maria read with Kishore?
qa.a: Maria read their duck picture book.

qa.q: How did Kishore seem to feel during the picture-book reading?
qa.a: He seemed curious and engaged, watching her mouth and trying the word.

qa.q: What was sensible about Maria's advice to Kishore's parents?
qa.a: Maria didn't forbid cartoons, but suggested watching with him and talking, because he learns best from live interaction.

qa.q: What is it like for Kishore's parents to receive this note?
qa.a: They may feel reassured and have a clear, gentle idea of how to help his words.

grounding: A daycare teacher notes a toddler learning words from live reading more than from cartoons.

passage:
During Navroz in Udvada, Tanuja's cousin called from abroad on a video call. Two-year-old Zubin stared at the little face on the phone.
Tanuja sat him on her lap and pointed. “See, Rustom Mama! Say hello!”
Zubin waved. Rustom waved back. Zubin laughed.
After two minutes, Zubin wriggled down and ran to the courtyard, where Dada was feeding the hens. He threw grain and shouted, “Chicken! Chicken!”

qa.q: Who did Zubin see on the phone?
qa.a: He saw Rustom Mama on the video call.

qa.q: How did Zubin feel when Rustom waved back?
qa.a: He was surprised and happy, laughing at the wave.

qa.q: What did Tanuja do well during the call?
qa.a: She held Zubin on her lap and named and pointed at things, so he wasn't watching alone.

qa.q: How might Rustom feel during the short call?
qa.a: He may feel happy to see Zubin, even if the toddler soon ran off to play.

grounding: A toddler shares a brief co-viewed video call and then learns most from live play.

passage:
Trisha, five, climbed into the auto after school in Mumbai and started talking before Samir could ask.
“First, we did colouring. Then Ms Pinto read the lion story. Then… no, wait, first was prayer. Then colouring. Then the lion story. Then lunch. Mira spilled her dal. At the end we sang the goodbye song.”
Samir laughed. “What happened to Mira's dal?”
“It went on her shoes! And then she cried. And then Ms Pinto wiped it.”

qa.q: What did Trisha say came first when she corrected herself?
qa.a: First was prayer, then colouring.

qa.q: How did Trisha feel telling her father about her day?
qa.a: She felt excited and eager, talking before Samir even asked.

qa.q: What could Samir do to support Trisha's storytelling?
qa.a: He could keep asking “then what happened?” and let her fix the order herself, as she did.

qa.q: How might Mira have felt when the dal spilled?
qa.a: She probably felt upset and embarrassed, which is why she cried.

grounding: A five-year-old retells her school day in order, correcting her own sequence.

passage:
“Nani, can I tell you the crow story?”
“Tell me, Ojas.”
“There was a crow. He was so thirsty. He found a pot, but the water was down, down.”
“And then?”
“Then he put stones inside. One, two, lots. And the water came up!”
“And then?”
Ojas thought. “Oh! First he was flying and looking. Then the pot. Then stones. And at the end he drank and flew away happy.”
Neelam clapped. “What a good story, beta.”

qa.q: What did the crow put inside the pot?
qa.a: He put stones inside.

qa.q: How did Ojas feel when he fixed the order of the story?
qa.a: He felt excited and proud, remembering the beginning and putting it in the right place.

qa.q: What did Neelam do that helped Ojas tell the story in order?
qa.a: She kept asking “And then?” so he could think about what came next.

qa.q: How might Neelam feel hearing Ojas tell the whole story?
qa.a: She feels proud and delighted, clapping for him.

grounding: A five-year-old retells a familiar story with a beginning, middle and end.

passage:
Class note, Monday. Teacher: Urmila.
At circle time, Thomas (six) wanted to tell us about his cousin's wedding. I gave him three picture cards: First, Next, Last.
He held the first card. “First we wore new clothes.” Next card: “Next the horse came with music.” Last card: “Last we ate ice cream and I danced.”
He looked very pleased. The others clapped.
Next step: more sequence cards for everyone this week.

qa.q: What cards did the teacher give Thomas?
qa.a: The teacher gave him three picture cards: First, Next, Last.

qa.q: How did Thomas feel after telling his story?
qa.a: He felt pleased and proud, especially when the others clapped.

qa.q: Why were the picture cards helpful for Thomas?
qa.a: They gave him a simple structure to tell events in order.

qa.q: How might the other children feel hearing Thomas's story?
qa.a: They probably enjoyed it and may be eager to tell their own stories with the cards 🙂

grounding: A teacher notes a six-year-old telling an event in order with sequence cards.

passage:
Monday: In the car, Abhinav, five, stared out of the window. “Abbu, why is the moon following us?”
Farhan smiled. “It's very, very far away.”
“But why does far make it follow?”
Wednesday: At home Abhinav asked why ice turns into water. Farhan put an ice cube on a plate. They watched.
“Why is it crying?”
“It's melting because it's warm.”
Saturday: Abhinav put two ice cubes out: one in the sun, one in the shade. “Abbu! The sun one melted first! Why?”

qa.q: Where did Abhinav put the two ice cubes on Saturday?
qa.a: One in the sun and one in the shade.

qa.q: How did Abhinav feel about the ice cubes on Saturday?
qa.a: He was excited and curious, eager to know why the sun one melted first.

qa.q: Which of Farhan's answers helped Abhinav most, and why?
qa.a: He let Abhinav watch the ice melt himself, so the boy began testing his own ideas.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel about Abhinav's endless “why”s?
qa.a: He may feel proud of his son's curiosity, even if sometimes a bit tired.

grounding: Over a week a five-year-old asks repeated why questions and begins to test the answers.

passage:
The power went off during dinner in their Delhi flat. The fan slowed and stopped.
“Mama, why did the fan stop?”
“No electricity, Leela.”
“Why no electricity?”
Amandeep was searching for the torch in the dark with one hand, holding the dal pot with the other. “The wires… maybe the rain.”
“Why does rain stop wires?”
Amandeep found the torch and switched it on. “Good question. Let's look out and see if other houses are dark too.”
Leela ran to the window. “All dark! Why?”

qa.q: What did Amandeep hold while searching for the torch?
qa.a: She held the dal pot with the other hand.

qa.q: How did Leela feel during the power cut?
qa.a: She was curious and interested, asking one question after another.

qa.q: How could a busy parent answer questions like Leela's?
qa.a: Like Amandeep, they can turn a question into a quick way to look and find out, such as checking if other houses are dark.

qa.q: How might Amandeep feel answering questions in the dark with a pot in her hand?
qa.a: She may feel a little stressed but also amused by Leela's curiosity.

grounding: During a power cut a four-year-old asks repeated why questions to understand what happened.

passage:
Tanvir, five, stood beside Madhav-kaka, the building watchman, as he waited for the lift.
“Why does the lift go up?”
“There's a big rope inside, pulling it.”
“Why doesn't it fall?”
“There are brakes.”
“Why?”
Madhav-kaka laughed. “So children like you are safe.”
The lift arrived. Tanvir got in, looked up at the ceiling, and asked, “Where is the rope? Why can't I see it?”

qa.q: Who did Tanvir stand beside?
qa.a: He stood beside Madhav-kaka, the building watchman.

qa.q: How did Tanvir feel about the lift?
qa.a: He was curious and a little amazed, asking many questions about how it works.

qa.q: What could Tanvir's family do to answer his questions?
qa.a: They could look at a simple picture of a lift with him or ask the watchman to show a safe look at the machine room.

qa.q: How does Madhav-kaka see Tanvir's questions?
qa.a: He finds them amusing and sweet, answering patiently and laughing.

grounding: A five-year-old asks repeated why questions to understand how a lift works.

passage:
On the bus home from school, Raghav, five, held Indu's hand and said, “Amma, listen. My poem for Independence Day.”
He said the first four lines slowly, looking out of the window. On the fifth he stopped. “Umm…”
Indu whispered the first word. “Tiranga…”
“Tiranga lehraye!” Raghav finished, and said the whole poem again, faster, tapping the beat on the seat.
By their stop, he had said it five times.

qa.q: How many times had Raghav said the poem by their stop?
qa.a: By their stop, he had said it five times.

qa.q: How did Raghav feel when he got stuck on the fifth line?
qa.a: He felt a little stuck and unsure, but then excited and confident when he remembered.

qa.q: What did Indu do that helped Raghav remember?
qa.a: She whispered only the first word, so he could find the rest himself.

qa.q: How might Raghav's teacher feel on Independence Day?
qa.a: The teacher may feel proud to hear him recite the whole poem with rhythm.

grounding: A five-year-old memorises a poem by repeating it and tapping the rhythm.

passage:
“Naveen, shall we do the rhyme?”
“Yes, Dadu!”
Arnab-dadu started. “Aay re aay, tiye…”
“Nayey chore Ganga dhiye!” Naveen shouted.
“Good! Next line?”

qa.q: How did Naveen feel when he remembered the line?

passage:

Pranav (five) has learned the whole morning song in two weeks. Today he sang all four verses without help, swaying.

qa.a: He learned the whole morning song in two weeks.

qa.q: How did Pranav seem to feel singing the song?
qa.a: He seemed happy and confident, swaying as he sang.

qa.q: What strategy did Pranav use when he forgot a word?
qa.a: He went back to the start of the verse and sang again until the word came.

qa.q: How might Pranav's parents feel reading this note?

grounding: A music teacher notes a five-year-old memorising songs and using rhythm to recall them.

passage:
In the market in Amman, Yara's red balloon slipped from her hand and floated up above the stalls.
Yara stamped her foot and opened her mouth to scream. Then she stopped.
“Mama,” she said, her lip shaking, “I am sad because my balloon went up and I can't get it.”
Dalia knelt and hugged her. “Thank you for telling me. That is sad.”
Yara watched the balloon until it was a tiny dot. “Bye, balloon.”

qa.q: What colour was Yara's balloon?
qa.a: It was red.

qa.q: How did Yara feel when the balloon floated away, and how did she show it?
qa.a: She felt sad and upset, and she named it in words instead of screaming.

qa.q: Why was Dalia's response helpful to Yara?
qa.a: She knelt, hugged her and thanked her for telling, which accepts the feeling and encourages her to name it again.

qa.q: What would change if Yara had screamed instead of speaking?
qa.a: Her mother might not have understood as quickly why she was upset.

grounding: A five-year-old names her sadness and its cause instead of only acting it out.

passage:
In the kindergarten at Kochi, there was a feelings chart on the wall with faces: happy, sad, angry, scared.
At play time, Anjali, five, came to Ms Ritu with her fists clenched.
“Use your words, Anjali.”
Anjali pointed to the angry face. “I am angry because Mohan took my spot at the window.”
Ms Ritu nodded. “Thank you for telling me. Let's go and talk to Mohan together.”
Anjali's fists opened.

qa.q: What faces were on the feelings chart?
qa.a: Happy, sad, angry, scared.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling when she came to Ms Ritu?
qa.a: She felt angry, with her fists clenched, because Mohan took her spot.

qa.q: How did the feelings chart and Ms Ritu help Anjali?
qa.a: The chart gave her a way to name her feeling, and Ms Ritu offered to help solve the problem.

qa.q: How might Mohan feel when Anjali and Ms Ritu come to talk?
qa.a: He might feel surprised or a bit worried, but talking may help him understand why Anjali was upset.

grounding: A five-year-old uses words to name and explain her anger at kindergarten.

passage:
I'm Usha, and I sit on the park bench most evenings. Yesterday I watched Tarun, six, playing near the swings.
A big brown dog came trotting in. Tarun froze. He didn't cry. He walked over to his father and pulled his sleeve.
“Papa, I'm scared because that dog is very big.”
His father lifted him up. They watched the dog together until it went away.
I don't know how he learned to say it so clearly. My grandsons just screamed.

qa.q: What colour was the dog?
qa.a: It was a big brown dog.

qa.q: How did Tarun feel when the dog came, and what did he do?
qa.a: He felt scared and froze, but then told his father in words why he was afraid.

qa.q: What did Tarun's father do that helped?
qa.a: He lifted Tarun up and watched the dog with him until it went away.

qa.q: How does Usha see Tarun's way of handling his fear?
qa.a: Usha is impressed and curious, comparing it with her grandsons who just screamed.

grounding: A park regular observes a six-year-old naming his fear and its reason to his father.

passage:
In their village near Bareilly, the goat chewed a hole in Tarun's new kite, and Tarun's face went red.
He stamped. He wanted to hit the goat.
Then he remembered what Rehana-khala, who lived next door, had shown him. He ran to the neem tree and sat in its shade. He breathed out slowly, like blowing out a candle. Once, twice, five times.
Rehana came out and sat beside him. “Better?”
“A bit,” Tarun said. “Can we fix the kite?”

qa.q: Where did Tarun sit to calm down?
qa.a: He sat in the shade of the neem tree.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling when the goat chewed his kite?
qa.a: He felt very angry, stamping and wanting to hit the goat.

qa.q: What calm-down strategy worked for Tarun, and why?
qa.a: Sitting in a quiet place and breathing out slowly like blowing a candle, which helped his anger settle.

qa.q: How might Rehana feel seeing Tarun use her idea?
qa.a: She likely feels pleased and proud that he remembered what she taught him.

grounding: A five-year-old uses a quiet spot and slow breathing to settle his anger.

passage:
In their terraced house in Birmingham, a clap of thunder shook the windows, and Siddiq, five, ran out of his room.
“Baba! I'm scared!”
Jamal opened his arms. Siddiq pressed his face into his father's chest.
“Let's breathe together,” Jamal said. “Smell the flower… blow the candle.”
They did it three times. Siddiq's shoulders came down.
Another rumble. Siddiq flinched but didn't run. “Smell the flower,” he whispered to himself.

qa.q: What did Jamal say to do when breathing?
qa.a: Smell the flower, blow the candle.

qa.q: How was Siddiq feeling when he heard the thunder?
qa.a: He felt scared and ran to his father.

qa.q: What helped Siddiq calm down?
qa.a: A hug from his father and breathing together three times.

qa.q: How might Jamal feel when Siddiq whispers the breathing words himself?
qa.a: He probably feels relieved and proud that Siddiq is learning to calm himself.

grounding: A five-year-old uses a hug and breathing to settle his fear during a storm.

passage:
At sports day practice in the school ground, Sarita, five, came last in the race. She threw her ribbon on the ground and shouted.
Mr Rafiq, her teacher, knelt beside her. “Do you want the calm corner?”
Sarita nodded, tears on her cheeks. She sat on the cushion under the tree where the class kept a soft toy and a picture of a turtle.
She hugged the toy and breathed. After a few minutes, she came back and picked up her ribbon.

qa.q: What did Sarita throw on the ground?
qa.a: She threw her ribbon on the ground.

qa.q: How did Sarita feel after coming last in the race?
qa.a: She felt angry and upset, with tears on her cheeks.

qa.q: How did the calm corner help Sarita?

On the verandah of a house in a Kerala village, Imran and Elizabeth, both five, played snakes and ladders.
Imran rolled a four. His counter landed on the big snake's head.
“No!” He looked at Elizabeth, then quickly moved his counter one square forward.
Elizabeth frowned. “That's cheating.”
Imran's ears went red. He moved it back and slid down the snake all the way to the bottom. “Okay. Your turn.”
Elizabeth rolled. Imran watched, arms crossed, but he waited.

qa.q: What did Imran roll?
qa.a: He rolled a four.

qa.q: How did Imran feel when Elizabeth said “That's cheating”?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, with red ears, but chose to play fair.

qa.q: What could an adult say to Imran after the game?
qa.a: They could tell him it was hard to slide down and that playing fair made the game fun for both.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth feel when Imran moves his counter back?
qa.a: She probably feels relieved and happy that the game is fair again.

grounding: A five-year-old stops himself from cheating and accepts the outcome of a game.

passage:
In a small square in Lisbon, Camila and Bilal, both five, played hopscotch with chalk.
Camila hopped to square six and her foot landed right on the line.
“Line!” Bilal said.
Camila stopped. “No, it wasn't.” She looked down. It was.
She sighed loudly. “Okay. Your turn.”
Bilal hopped all the way to ten and back. Camila clapped, a bit slowly.
Then she took the stone and began again from one.

qa.q: Where did Camila's foot land?
qa.a: Her foot landed right on the line.

qa.q: How did Camila feel when she had to give up her turn?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and frustrated, sighing loudly, but accepted it.

qa.q: What could Bilal do to keep the game friendly?
qa.a: He could cheer for Camila on her next turn so she feels included.

qa.q: How might Bilal feel when Camila accepts the rule?
qa.a: He probably feels the game is fair and enjoys playing with her.

grounding: A five-year-old accepts losing her turn in hopscotch without cheating.

passage:
In the school hall, Ms Keerthana played music for musical chairs. When it stopped, Ira, five, was left standing.
Her lip wobbled. She tried to squeeze onto the edge of Kavin's chair.
“Ira,” said Ms Keerthana gently. “You're out this round.”
Ira stood still, fists tight. Then she took a big breath and walked to the side.
“Want to be my music helper?” Ms Keerthana asked.
Ira nodded and pressed the button for the next round, smiling a little.

qa.q: What did Ira try to squeeze onto?
qa.a: She tried to squeeze onto the edge of Kavin's chair.

qa.q: How did Ira feel when she was left standing?
qa.a: She felt upset and disappointed, with a wobbling lip and tight fists.

qa.q: What did Ms Keerthana do that helped Ira accept being out?
qa.a: She calmly stated the rule and then gave Ira a helper role, so she still felt part of the game.

qa.q: How might Kavin feel when Ira tries to share his chair?
qa.a: He might feel annoyed or confused, since he won his chair fairly.

grounding: A five-year-old accepts being out in musical chairs with a teacher's gentle support.
